newsitem.title: INDIA: Moody's Indian report seen having little impact.
newsitem.headline: Moody's Indian report seen having little impact.

text.p: The unfavourable outlook given to India's sovereign rating by Moody's Investors Service Inc probably will not have an immediate impact on inflows of capital or the cost of external borrowings, bankers and analysts said on Tuesday.

They also questioned whether the Moody's report, released on Monday, took account of policy measures announced in the federal budget on February 28. These were received favourably by Indian financial markets.
"We are frankly surprised both at the action as well as the timing," said R. Ravimohan, managing director of the Credit Rating Information Services of India Ltd (CRISIL).
Moody's said in its report that India had an unstable political environment and directionless economic policies.
It said a "deterioration in India's macroeconomic balances" had led it to take an unfavourable outlook on the nation's Baa3 sovereign rating.
"It is not clear at the moment but it appears that this decision was taken before the budget," Ravimohan said.

When Finance minister P. Chidambaram presented the 1997/98 (April-March) budget to parliament on February 28, he announced cuts in tariffs, corporate and personal taxes and steps to improve fiscal discipline.
Shares at the Bombay Stock Exchange surged 16 percent in post-budget euphoria before profit-taking trimmed gains.

"I think there have been a number of positive announcements in the budget," Ravimohan said. "It has renewed the commitment to reforms, it has attempted to be progressive by reducing tariffs and has also taken some tough decisions to tighten fiscal discipline."
The impact on inflows into the country as well as India's external borrowings was expected to be minor.
"The reports are not very clear at the moment but I do not think India's rating has been changed," said a research head at a foreign investment firm.
"There is a difference between giving an unfavourable outlook and lowering the rating," he said. "I do not see much of an impact."
"It won't impact FDI (foreign direct investment) flows into infrastructure," Abhay Rangnekar, director, structured finance at Barclays Bank Plc in Bombay said.
"That's more a function of implementation of government policies," he said, adding that FDI flows to some south-east Asian countries were not affected by fluctuating ratings.
Some bankers said the reaction of export credit agencies would be watched keenly.
"If they decide to raise insurance premiums, it will ultimately result in a hike in the cost of Indian firms' external commercial borrowings," said a banker who declined to be identified.
Other bankers differed, saying there would be no impact.

"International lenders in the syndicated loan and debt capital markets are very knowledgeable and understand the Indian landscape thoroughly," said Rana Kapoor, general manager corporate finance at ANZ Grindlays Investment Bank.
"The competition for Indian issues in the syndicated loan and debt capital markets is intense," he said.
"International investors have faith in the sustainability of economic reforms, the quality of Indian borrowers and in the policies of the government," he added.
"There will be no impact from this development."
